name: Open-Closed Principle
intent: Add new behaviour by adding new code instead of editing code that is already tested and in production, by putting an abstraction at the point where change is actually expected.
scenario: A shop prices orders with a discount function that switches on customer type: regular and member. Over the next year marketing asks for 1, then 3, then 6 more rule types. The team compares the growing switch, a strategy-style design with one class per rule, and a plug-in framework with factories, descriptors and a loader that someone built for the two rules that existed at the start.
problem: Every new rule type that is added by editing the same function puts all the existing rules at risk: the code is open to every change and closed to none. A new branch can break an old one, all the old tests must run again, and the function keeps growing. The cure people reach for is an abstraction, but an abstraction built before the variation is known adds files, names and indirection for changes that may never come, and when the real change is a different one, the abstraction is in the wrong place and is harder to change than the switch was.

howItWorks.title: Name the change you expect
howItWorks.text: Open-closed is always relative to a kind of change: closed against new discount rules, say, but not against everything. Pick it from evidence, such as the second or third time you edit the same function for the same kind of request. A design cannot be closed against changes nobody has seen, and guessing leads to speculative abstractions.

howItWorks.title: Put the variation behind an interface
howItWorks.text: Define the small contract that every rule satisfies, for example a DiscountRule with one method that takes the order and returns an amount. The pricing engine depends only on that contract and applies whichever rules it is given. It never inspects the customer type, so the engine does not change when a rule is added.

howItWorks.title: Extend by adding a class
howItWorks.text: A new rule is a new class, with its own tests, and a registration somewhere. The tested code stays as it was: the old rules are not in any edited file, so their branches cannot be broken by accident, and only the new rule's tests are new. The registration is itself an edit to an existing file, so closed does not mean never edited, it means not edited in the places that hold the logic.

howItWorks.title: Weigh the cost of the abstraction
howItWorks.text: The interface, the engine and the registry are extra files that exist even when there are only two rules. With a plug-in framework of factories, descriptors and a loader, the 2 rules cost 11 files instead of 1. The abstraction pays off only when enough variants arrive, and in the example the strategy-style design overtakes the switch from 3 added rules and the framework from 7.

howItWorks.title: Expect to be wrong sometimes
howItWorks.text: When a change arrives that the abstraction did not anticipate, such as every rule now needing the customer's country, the cost can be higher than before: the interface, the engine and every rule class change. Refactor the abstraction to fit what you learn. Waiting for the second or third real case before abstracting is a common way to find the right place for the seam.

pros: New behaviour arrives as new code with its own tests, leaving tested code alone
Existing rules are not in the edited code, so a slip cannot change them
Teams can add variants without understanding every existing one
The decision logic stops growing as a single large if/else or switch
cons: An interface, an engine and a registry cost files and indirection before they save anything
The abstraction is right only for the kind of change it was designed for
Registration still edits an existing file, and a change to the interface touches every implementation
Reading a flow that is spread over many small rule classes takes longer than reading one function
whenToUse: The same function has been edited for the same kind of request several times
New variants arrive often and each one should have its own tests
Different people add variants, and should not need to read all the others
whenNotToUse: A short switch over two or three cases that rarely changes: leave it
Before the second or third real variant, when you would be guessing where the variation lies
When the likely change is a different one, such as a new input to every rule, that the abstraction would not absorb
pitfalls: Predicting variation that never comes: a plug-in framework for two rules that stay two
Letting an if/else or switch grow with every new type, so each addition edits and risks every existing branch
Reading closed as never edit: registration, wiring and interface changes are normal edits
Putting the abstraction in the wrong place, so a different change edits the interface and every implementation
Building the abstraction first and finding the real variants later, when the second case would have shown the seam
Treating every if statement as a violation: a stable branch that has not changed in years is fine

quiz.question: A function has a switch on customer type with 2 branches. A new customer type arrives every month. What is the main risk of simply adding a branch each time?
options: Each edit puts every existing branch inside the changed code, so old rules can break by accident.
The compiler slows down once a switch passes a certain number of branches.
Switch statements cannot call other classes, so the logic cannot be reused.
A switch hides which customer types exist, so no tests can be written for it.
quiz.explanation: Editing the same function for every rule exposes all the old branches to a slip and forces their tests to run again. A switch can be tested and does not slow the compiler. The cost is the exposure and the growth, not the language feature.

quiz.question: A team builds a plug-in framework with factories, descriptors and a config loader for 2 discount rules. Two years later there are still 2 rules. What is the best description of what happened?
options: The framework worked: it kept the code closed against modification.
The framework was too small, and it should have been built with more extension points.
The team paid for flexibility it never used: a speculative abstraction.
Plug-in frameworks always fail because configuration is hard to test.
quiz.explanation: An abstraction is a bet on a kind of change. With 2 rules that stay 2, the extra files and indirection are pure cost, and a plain switch would have been easier to read. Frameworks are not always wrong, they pay off only when variants arrive.

quiz.question: A strategy-style design has one class per rule behind a DiscountRule interface. A new requirement says every rule must now receive the customer's country. What happens?
options: Nothing, because adding a rule never changes existing code.
Only the new rule classes need to change, because old ones ignore the country.
Only the registry changes, because it creates the rules and can pass the country.
The interface and the engine change, and so does every rule class: the seam was in the wrong place.
quiz.explanation: The abstraction is closed against new rules, not against a new input that every rule needs. A change to the interface touches every implementation, which can cost more than the same change in a plain switch. Closed means closed against a chosen kind of change.
